item.fts_geology.field_guide.tooltip: Comprehensive field manual for reading plates, landforms, and instruments
book.fts_geology.page.1:
§lFT's Geology§r
§oField Guide§r

Beneath this world lies not a random noise map, but a thermodynamic simulation of a living planet.

Rigid tectonic plates drift across the mantle. Where they collide, pull apart, or grind past each other, landforms are born.

This guide explains how to read the landscape.
book.fts_geology.page.2:
§lI. The Landscape§r
§oFault Scarps & Rifts§r

In real geology, a fault is a fracture where crustal blocks slip. When crust stretches, blocks drop along normal faults, forming steep scarps and rift valleys.

In this mod, look for stepped cliffs where strata do not match across a line. Scarps mark active plate boundaries under extensional tension.
book.fts_geology.page.3:
§lI. The Landscape§r
§oMantle Plumes§r

Plumes are buoyant columns of superheated mantle rising from deep within the Earth, independent of boundaries.

They create broad topographic domes, high ground heat flow, and basaltic shield chains trailing with plate drift. If you find clustered hot springs and lava flows in an interior, you stand over a plume.
book.fts_geology.page.4:
§lI. The Landscape§r
§oSubduction Margins§r

When heavy oceanic crust meets lighter continental crust, it dives beneath it into the mantle, forming a deep ocean trench.

As it sinks, released water lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge above, feeding a volcanic arc 100-300 blocks inland. Steep stratovolcanoes and deep quakes mark these violent margins.
book.fts_geology.page.5:
§lII. Instruments§r
§oGeologist's Hammer§r

A geologist strikes rock not to break it but to see a fresh face and name its class: volcanic, plutonic, sedimentary or metamorphic.

Right-click a rock to read its origin and the beds under it, in real metres. Strike an ore mineral and the hammer prospects it: see the next page.
book.fts_geology.page.6:
§lII. Instruments§r
§oProspecting§r

Ore is the residue of a process, and its minerals show which. The rusty pyrite halo, the green and blue of oxidised copper, a quartz vein: each belongs to a system the plates made.

Strike one with the hammer. It names the system and the richest ore within 16 blocks and 48 down, how much and how deep, and a trail of glints leads off toward it.
book.fts_geology.page.7:
§lII. Instruments§r
§oCore Drill§r

Hold it against the ground: in two seconds it bores 64 blocks down and brings up a §lCore Sample§r, each bed with its thickness, any deposit named for what laid it, and the water table.

Right-click a core to read it again. A line of cores across a valley shows the beds bend and break.
book.fts_geology.page.8:
§lII. Instruments§r
§oGeothermal Probe§r

Reads the heat flow under you, and how well the ground suits a volcano, a geyser field or hot springs.

It tells whether a well bored straight down would reach a hot water reservoir, how deep, and what a turbine would make there; steam rises where one would pay. It also points to the nearest hot ground.
book.fts_geology.page.9:
§lII. Instruments§r
§oGeological Map§r

A map, an amethyst shard and a copper ingot. Open it and carry it: it fills in with the rock under the soil. Red volcanic, pink granite, purple metamorphic, yellow sandstone.

Faults are coloured lines, with arrows for how the plates move; dark stripes mark an active fault zone.
book.fts_geology.page.10:
§lII. Instruments§r
§oFault Compass§r

Modelled on a Brunton field compass. It measures the strike — the compass bearing along the boundary plane.

Use it in hand to sample your tectonic plate: its velocity, drift heading, and distance to the nearest boundary. It reveals whether a fault is locked and accumulating strain, or creeping and quietly slipping without quakes.
book.fts_geology.page.11:
§lII. Instruments§r
§oSeismograph§r

A drum that records the waves. The fast P wave arrives first, the slower S wave later: the gap gives the distance, the swing the magnitude.

The alert comes the moment the fault breaks, the shaking with the S wave, so the siren sounds for longer the further the station is. Redstone runs full through the warning.

Right-click it with paper and it prints its record as a book: the quakes day by day, the latest in full, and a restless volcano's swelling and swarm hour by hour.
book.fts_geology.page.12:
§lIII. Hot Springs§r
§oHydrothermal Origin§r

Groundwater seeps miles deep along fault fractures, is heated by magma or the geothermal gradient, and rises buoyantly.

§lStage 1: Nascent Pool§r
Boiling water (>85°C) breaches the surface, scouring a clear pool into bedrock. Dissolved silica and carbonate are supercharged in solution under immense hydrostatic pressure.
book.fts_geology.page.13:
§lIII. Hot Springs§r
§oStages 2 & 3§r

§lStage 2: Microbial Mats§r
As outflow cools, extremophile bacteria colonise thermal zones: vivid orange/yellow carotenoids in warm water (60-75°C), brown/green mats in cooler shallows (<55°C).

§lStage 3: Sinter & Terraces§r
Silica precipitates as porous chalky sinter; carbonates build stepped travertine terraces. Acid steam turns rock into bubbling mud pots.
book.fts_geology.page.14:
§lIII. Hot Springs§r
§oStage 4: Fumaroles§r

When thermal output drops or the water table falls below the heating zone, pools boil dry.

The system enters its senescent stage: pressurized steam and hydrogen sulfide hiss through tapering fumarole chimneys.

Native sulfur crystals sublimate directly from the volcanic gases around the vent rim, crusting the rocks in brilliant yellow.
book.fts_geology.page.15:
§lIV. Volcanoes§r
§oThe Setting Decides§r

A volcano's shape is not picked from a list; it is dictated by tectonic chemistry. Silica content determines magma viscosity.

§lShield Volcanoes§r
Mantle plumes and oceanic rifts melt peridotite into low-silica, fluid basalt. Lava flows for thousands of blocks before freezing, building broad, gently sloping oceanic shield mountains.
book.fts_geology.page.16:
§lIV. Volcanoes§r
§oStrato & Fissures§r

§lStratovolcanoes§r
Subduction melts wet crust into viscous, gas-rich andesite and rhyolite. Trapped volatiles burst violently, building steep composite cones of alternating ash and viscous lava.

§lFissure Eruptions§r
Divergent rifts crack the crust along linear dikes. Basalt fountains along miles of fissure, flooding valleys without building a central cone.
book.fts_geology.page.17:
§lIV. Volcanoes§r
§oCalderas§r

The most catastrophic volcanic structure. A massive shallow magma reservoir evacuates rapidly during an ultra-Plinian eruption.

Deprived of hydraulic support beneath, the entire volcanic summit collapses into the empty magma chamber. What remains is a vast, circular sunken basin rimmed by steep fracture walls, often hosting resurgent domes and lakes.
book.fts_geology.page.18:
§lIV. Volcanoes§r
§oWarnings & Hazards§r

Before an eruption, rising magma sets off a swarm of small quakes that seismographs record; springs steam harder and the probe reads the ground swelling.

§lPyroclastic flows§r of burning ash race down the valleys of strato and caldera volcanoes: get to high ground. Unseen CO2 lies in the crater and round vents, in hollows too when it wakes; it snuffs torches, and dead ground marks it. Clear ash off flat roofs; the rain washes it away in time.
book.fts_geology.page.19:
§lV. Earthquakes§r
§oElastic Rebound & Rifts§r

Plates move constantly, but friction locks boundary faults. Elastic strain stores in the rock for years until stress overcomes friction: the fault snaps, releasing energy as seismic waves.

§lRift Quakes§r
Plates pull apart. The hanging wall slides downward along normal faults. Produces shallow, sharp tremors that open fissures and lower graben floors.
book.fts_geology.page.20:
§lV. Earthquakes§r
§oCollision & Transform§r

§lTransform Quakes§r
Plates grind past each other, shearing ridges and streams sideways; where the fault steps aside a basin drops: the Bursa plain.

§lCollision & Megathrusts§r
The squeezed plate snaps: the largest quakes. Everest's and K2's thrusts come up far to their south; the Matterhorn's fault runs down the valley north of it.
book.fts_geology.page.21:
§lV. Earthquakes§r
§oWaves & Intensity§r

The shaking is felt far beyond the fault: a magnitude 6 some nine hundred blocks out, a great quake thousands.

First the P wave, a jolt and a boom, and a warning of the seconds left; then the S wave, the shaking proper. A line tells how hard it shook where you stand, on the Mercalli scale.

Every stretch of a fault keeps its own clock: the longer since it broke, the likelier it is to break, wherever you are. On a boundary a quake is felt every few days, a thousand blocks off every week or two; a seismograph records all within four thousand blocks.
book.fts_geology.page.22:
§lV. Earthquakes§r
§oBuildings§r

Each block carries all that stands on it. Shaken sand and gravel carry nothing, glass and wool little, wood more, stone and brick most, obsidian and metal all.

A column that cannot hold its load comes down with all it bears; overhangs fall, slender towers topple, and what stands on the rupture itself is torn apart.
book.fts_geology.page.23:
§lV. Earthquakes§r
§oAftershocks§r

A big quake does not end at once. The fault slips again, three to five times worth feeling, most of them soon after, the largest about a magnitude and a fifth below the main shock.

Now and then a great quake is foretold by a smaller one on the same spot, minutes before.
book.fts_geology.page.24:
§lV. Earthquakes§r
§oLiquefaction§r

Shaken hard, wet sand stops being ground. Along rivers, on floodplains and by the sea, sand boils open and water wells up through them.

What stands on it sinks, up to four blocks and more on one side, so a house leans; whoever stands on it is held fast.
book.fts_geology.page.25:
§lV. Earthquakes§r
§oLandslides§r

Steep slopes lose their cover in strong shaking: soil, scree, sand and snow slide down as one mass, trees and all, heap up at the foot and leave a raw scar of rock.

The steeper and the wetter the slope, the likelier. A slope anyone built on is left alone. With Dynamic Trees, strong shaking fells its trees.
book.fts_geology.page.26:
§lVI. Geothermal Power§r
§oTurbine & Well§r

A turbine runs on the steam of a hot water reservoir. Dig down under it and line the hole with §lWell Casing§r.

A short well to a hot spring's bed gives part power; one bored to the chamber 30-60 blocks under a spring gives full power.
book.fts_geology.page.27:
§lVI. Geothermal Power§r
§oGeysers & Output§r

Set a turbine straight on an active geyser's vent and it caps the geyser: no more eruptions, all its steam goes to the turbine.

FE leaves from the sides and top. Turbines close together share one reservoir. Right-click one to see why it runs or not.
book.fts_geology.page.28:
§lVII. Rivers & Soil§r
§oRivers§r

Rivers rise at springs in the hills and run to the sea, cutting their own valleys. Their water never floods or drains away: it stands as the river does, stepping down the valley, and carries a swimmer gently along.

A pump draws plain water from it, and the river stays.
book.fts_geology.page.29:
§lVII. Rivers & Soil§r
§oFloodplains§r

A river in flood spreads its silt over the plain beside it, and every flood leaves fresh, rich ground: the Nile was farmed first for it.

On the §lAlluvial Plain§r, crops on tilled soil ripen half again as fast.
book.fts_geology.page.30:
§lVII. Rivers & Soil§r
§oKarst§r

Where marble or calcite lies under a plateau, water eats the rock away. Sinkholes pock the ground, and now and then a small river falls into a swallow hole, runs on in a cave under its dry valley and comes out further down, level with the river below.

§l/geology find swallowhole§r
book.fts_geology.page.31:
§lVII. Rivers & Soil§r
§oWater in the Ground§r

The ground keeps its rain, and a game day is a week of its time. A dry spell browns the grass in days; six days more with the roots at the wilting point and it dies back to bare soil in patches, and no grass spreads until the rain comes back. Grass by water stays green, a dry field's crops stop, and rain standing for days in a hollow turns it to mud, dry again after a drought.

Water poured on dry soil soaks away, sand fastest, clay slowest; a pond, a river and the sea stay. Mulch keeps the soil under it wet.

(soilWaterChangesGround, off by default)
book.fts_geology.page.32:
§lVII. Rivers & Soil§r
§oWells§r

Set a §lWell Pump§r on Well Casing that goes down below the water table. On FE, or Electrodynamics' 120 V, it lifts the water out of its sides and top.

The rock at the well's foot sets the pace: gravel and sand give freely, hard rock and clay little. The table sinks in a cone round a busy well and fills back in when it stops. With Create, a pipe's end buried below the table draws water too.

A hot spring whose water a busy well takes stops flowing, and a geyser drawn down only steams, until the cone fills back in.

§oDams§r

Wall a river across and it fills up behind the wall, a layer at a time, to the wall's top or the valley's lowest side. Build it thick: stone about as thick as the water is high, concrete half that, earth three times. While it fills, the river below runs a block lower; once full, it spills over the crest's lowest point, where a Create water wheel turns, and a notch cut in the crest lets it down to there. A dam too thin creaks and leaks, then breaks, and a wave floods the valley below for a minute. Water brought onto a thin cave roof can bring it down, and a well that drains a limestone cave warns before its sinkhole opens: the ground cracks, then a ring of it sinks.

§oSea Water§r

Sea water is salt: it does not water farmland, and a bucket filled at sea comes up as sea water. Rivers, lakes, springs, wells and reservoirs are fresh.
book.fts_geology.page.33:
§lVII. Rivers & Soil§r
§oRain & Floods§r

Rain comes in storms that drift with the wind: showers that pass in an hour, fronts that rain most of a day, and in a wet spell slow rains that hang on for days. Each region has its wet and dry spells, weeks long; wet lands get more rain than dry ones, a desert hardly any, and a mountainside facing the wind more than the lee behind it.

After rain, water stands in the hollows of ground that cannot drink it: rock, clay, a path, soaked loam. It dries from its edges.

Hard rain on soaked ground sends a river a block or two over its banks until the rain stops; in a narrow valley it comes as a flash flood. Dig through a river's bank and it runs out into the gap. A busy well can dry up a small stream near it.
book.fts_geology.page.34:
§lVIII. Commands§r
§oFinding§r

For operators.

§l/geology find <setting> [tp]§r
Nearest subduction, rift, collision, transform, hotspot, lava tube, valley, sinkhole, swallow hole, Everest, K2 or Matterhorn.

§l/geology field [type] [tp]§r
Nearest large volcano: strato, shield, caldera, active, dormant...
book.fts_geology.page.35:
§lVIII. Commands§r
§oReading the Ground§r

§l/geology plate§r  the plate and boundary here.
§l/geology suitability§r  volcano, geyser and spring scores.
§l/geology column§r  the section from surface to bedrock, deposits and water table.
§l/geology map [scale]§r  a map of the plates and faults.
§l/geology water§r  the water in the ground here.
book.fts_geology.page.36:
§lVIII. Commands§r
§oQuakes & Features§r

§l/geology quake [type [magnitude]]§r  a quake here.
§l/geology quake cancel§r  stops them.
§l/geology quake aftershocks [clear]§r  the shocks still to come.
§l/geology place <feature> [medium]§r  a geyser, spring or volcano.
§l/geology deepgen [radius]§r  rebuild the deep geology.
§l/geology storms [spawn <strength> [radius]]§r  the weather here, or a storm over you.
